articles.title: Island hopping through stone-age history in Ireland, Wales and the Isle of Man
articles.summary: Exploring prehistory sites around the Irish Sea – that were old even before the pyramids were built – throws a magical light on our ancestors. The guide was adamant. “I’ve picked human teeth out of there and I’m not doing it again.” The small group of tourists looked suitably aghast, except the…
body: “So, if anyone is planning to leave human remains in this ancient place,” went on the guide, throwing the boy a stern look, “I say, DON’T.”

The plush visitor centre had been informative but had not conveyed the deep atavistic intensity that drives such tributes. There was magic here. I wanted to feel it. I had a hunch this boy was in touch with it.
“As for pets,” said our guide, “I want no dog or cat ashes either.”

The boy was drumming his hands on his knees, hearing an unheard rhythm. We were about to walk up to the hallowed tumulus with its 19-metre-long passageway that leads to the central chamber, but our guide was determined to get that boy’s attention. “There,” she shouted. The boy’s head shot up. She was pointing at a set of wheelie bins in the corner. “I can promise you,” she went on, grimly, “that if I find your granny’s remains inside my Neolithic chamber, then her last resting place will be that green wheelie bin.”

articles.title: ‘Digging the grave of my profession’: the Hollywood creatives training AI to do their jobs
articles.summary: Amid a jobs slump, award-winning writers, directors and producers taking on sometimes lucrative temp work teaching AI skills such as screenwriting and production. Hollywood creatives are taking gig work to train AI models to replicate their skills in a bid to offset tightening earnings in a trend…
body: Experienced and award-winning writers, directors and producers are being paid from $12 to $200 an hour to teach AI models the intricacies of their jobs, from writing a screenplay to devising a shooting schedule.

With feelings ranging from fatalism to guilt, the creatives have signed up with some of the booming training agencies, which have contracts with the biggest AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI, to pass on hard-won human skills in industries such as finance, health, law and social work.

While they wait for entertainment industry work, they give notes on the AI systems’ attempts to do the tasks they would hope to be paid for themselves. It comes amid a slump in jobs in the motion picture and sound recording industries, where AI is starting to take roles from actors, editors and special effects artists. Netflix this month revealed it used AI in 300 of its 1,000 titles in 2026, and directors including Ron Howard are starting to embrace the technology.
“It’s very production specific,” said Ruth Fowler, a screenwriter and producer in Los Angeles. “It’s teaching it how to take our jobs.”

articles.title: ‘It exists only for pleasure’: does ice-cream have a future in the age of wellness fads and weight-loss drugs?
articles.summary: As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs. Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?
body: A slop bucket full of Viennetta overrun stood at the side of the conveyer belt and I fought a strong urge to squelch my fingers into it. Later, the factory operations manager allowed me to push my whole hand into the slop bucket up to the wrist and then lick my hand at a sink, before washing it and resuming the tour.

Such drugs are not the only problem ice-cream makers have to contend with. In recent years, as wellness culture has gained momentum, a growing obsession with protein and fibre has changed the way we eat. Protein is touted as a magical cure for all manner of ills: perimenopause, anxiety, the urge to have a nap at 3pm. The price of whey – a yellowish, dusty, protein-rich powder made from curdled milk – is at an all-time global high and the US is in the grip of a shortage of cottage cheese, which is higher in protein and lower in fat than normal cheese. Demand has become so frenzied that people trade conspiracy theories about its scarcity online.
points: As fitness-conscious consumers turn away from processed foods, the industry is scrambling for new ideas, including nutrient-rich lollies and protein-packed tubs.
Will they take the fun out of this summer treat?

articles.title: Tim Dowling: my working holiday just isn’t working
articles.summary: The weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing, but I cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting I’m on holiday. In the summer of 1995, I went on a family holiday to Portugal.
body: “Sure,” I said. I broke the news, packed my things, flew to London and, the next day, to LA.

While no one who knows me would suggest I am overburdened by ambition, I still cling to the freelancer’s habit of never quite admitting to being on holiday: I bring work with me, I still accept assignments while I’m away, and I’m always a little cagey regarding my whereabouts.

On Friday an email arrives, asking if I’m available to go on the radio next week. I know I should admit that I’m on holiday in the country, in a remote cottage with no phone reception and ropey internet, poorly tethered to civilisation by a mile of copper wire. And so, on balance, no thanks, maybe next time.

Over the weekend guests arrive, friends on their way somewhere else. The weather is unrelentingly glorious, the views are amazing and I’m worrying about how I’m going to manage a live radio interview three days hence.

articles.title: 29 Easy Chicken Breast Recipes for Fall
articles.summary: Like saucy chicken stroganoff, miso chicken soup with squash, and cranberry chicken stir-fry.
body: In fall, chicken breasts are an easy starting point for all kinds of dinners: crispy cutlets, quick weeknight skillet meals, cozy soups, saucy chicken Parm—and on warm early-fall evenings, there’s still time for one last round of grilled chicken.

Learning how to cook chicken breasts so that they stay moist and tender doesn’t take much practice, just a little technique. Start by buying the best chicken breast you can find. Then follow our tips for frying the crispiest chicken cutlets, learn the key to the juiciest grilled chicken, or check out almost every other way to cook chicken breast.

Because they’re leaner than thighs, chicken breasts can easily overcook. Use an instant-read thermometer to check for doneness (chicken breasts are safely cooked when the thickest part reaches 165°F), and let the meat rest before slicing so the juices redistribute. Sauces and marinades can also help keep chicken breasts flavorful and juicy.

articles.title: Bridal Perfume: How to Choose the Right Fragrance for Your Wedding Day
articles.summary: What is the best fragrance for a wedding day? Five experts share their best tips for choosing a bridal perfume that will allow you to relive the cherished moment again and again.
body: One thing I would happily add to our “ magical DIY wedding under the stars ” on my dad’s ranch? An entirely new-to-me fragrance to help, a decade later, step directly through a portal to that party. Bluebonnets and bonfire smoke set the mood then, and camping out during Texas wildflower season can’t (yet!) be bottled. If I’d chosen to add Frédéric Malle and perfumer Dominique Ropion’s award-winning Portrait of A Lady eau de parfum to my stroll down the grassy aisle, could I now be transported from the comfort of a sectional with a single spritz? Maybe, according to some experts.

“Scent can be a powerful trigger of certain memories,” says Matthew Robison, assistant professor in the department of psychology at the University of Notre Dame. “We remember events with all their associated features, not only the sensory experience, but also the emotions we were experiencing at the time,” he explains, adding that memory is naturally associative, building connections between these sensory experiences and the people, places, and events surrounding them.

articles.title: Your Home’s Getting Dumber—and That’s a Good Thing
articles.summary: Here’s why analog is all the rage, according to top interior designers.
body: In an era when technology appears to have a chokehold on society, it’s natural to assume everything is possible through a tap, swipe, or AI prompt. However, when it comes to a well-appointed home, designers say: Not so fast. While some crave the human touch of hand-painted murals or a masterfully planned plate wall, a growing number of people are sidestepping the smart house for a more primitive setup. Goodbye, intelligent devices and Bluetooth-enabled everything. Welcome back, pared-back appliances and mechanical systems.

Call it what you want—“dumb homes,” “analog interiors,” or “lo-fi spaces”—but many are yearning for a simpler time. Before screens and Siri, to be precise. For Bari Jerauld, founder of Blank Slate Studio, the shift is a “response to overstimulation.”

“We spend so much of our lives on screens and in fast-moving digital environments, so the home has become the one place people desperately want to feel the opposite,” the London-based designer explains. “People are asking for warmth, character, and rooms that feel as though they have a history.”
